content: Koplik's spots are small, irregular, red lesions that feature a tiny bluish-white speck in the center of each spot. These lesions are typically observed on the buccal mucosa (the inner lining of the cheeks) and the lingual mucosa (the mucous membrane of the tongue). They are considered pathognomonic for the early stages of measles, meaning their presence is a definitive diagnostic sign of the disease. These spots are named after Henry Koplik (1858–1927), an American pediatrician who first described them in 1896. Koplik's spots often appear a few days before the characteristic measles rash develops, making them a valuable early clinical indicator, especially in children who are known to have been exposed to the measles virus. While Henry Koplik is credited with their detailed description, earlier observations of similar phenomena were made by other physicians. Some authors attribute the first description of these spots to Reubold in Würzburg in 1854, while others credit Johann Andreas Murray (1740–1791). Prior to Koplik's work, the German internist Carl Jakob Adolf Christian Gerhardt (1833–1902) described similar findings in 1874, as did the Danish physician N. Flindt in 1879. Additionally, the Russian physician Nicolai Feodorowitsch von Filatov (1847–1902) documented equivalent observations in 1897.
